title: Measles Killed 32 Baiga Children in Madhya Pradesh as Vaccination Lagged
excerpt: In Balaghat's forest blocks, measles-rubella coverage ran between 49% and 70% — far below the WHO's 95% herd-immunity threshold — and distance, migration and fragile trust kept children unprotected.
body:
• A measles outbreak in Birsa block of Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh, has reportedly killed 32 children from the Baiga community since May 2026, according to a Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance report.
  • An investigation by the Central National Joint Outbreak Response Team found first-dose measles-rubella coverage of 51% in Baihar block and 64.8% in Birsa block between April 2025 and March 2026 — far below the 95% two-dose threshold the World Health Organization sets for herd immunity.
  • Health workers cite distance, seasonal migration, language barriers and fragile trust: families initially turned to traditional healers, and some hid their children when health teams arrived.
  • Parents unsure of a child's vaccination status can check the child's immunisation card and ask their local ASHA worker or ANM about missed doses — officials in Balaghat have run evening vaccination sessions and door-to-door screening since the outbreak.

A desolate kind of calm has settled over the forests of Birsa block, in Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh. Underneath it is a grim figure: 32 children have reportedly died there since May 2026 in a measles outbreak, according to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

The children who died belonged to the Korku Bundari and Songadda areas — parts of Birsa block inhabited by the Baiga community. The skin rashes some children developed led locals to blame Mata ka prakop, a belief that attributes measles to the wrath of a goddess. Instead of going to health centres, families initially turned to traditional healers. When health workers eventually reached the forest villages, many families hid their children and refused to allow medical examinations. By that time, eight children had already died. The toll quadrupled before the outbreak was quelled.

A disease of poverty and social exclusion

The Baigas are classified in India as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, reflecting not just their poverty but also their distinct language, traditions and forest-based way of life, which leave them prone to exclusion from mainstream services. High rates of malnutrition, a lack of clean drinking water and residence in remote areas mean Baiga children are disproportionately at risk from infectious diseases, and vaccination is their most critical form of protection.

The investigating team found 604 children in various Anganwadi areas of Birsa block suffering from severe acute malnutrition, and 1,985 children suffering from moderate acute malnutrition. Malnutrition leaves children at greater risk of complications and death in an outbreak, ANM Asha Maravi told Gavi.

Coverage of 49–70%, against a 95% threshold

According to the Central National Joint Outbreak Response Team's investigation, between April 2025 and March 2026 the coverage for the first dose of the measles-rubella vaccine in Baihar block stood at 51%, and the second dose at 49%. In Birsa block, the figures were 64.8% and 65%. The World Health Organization reports 95% coverage with both doses as the threshold for herd immunity. There was some improvement between April and July 2026, but first-dose coverage in Birsa reached only 70.4% by mid-year.

Research on tribal communities elsewhere in India points the same way. A study of children in tribal Odisha published in the Indian Journal of Medical Research found two-dose measles vaccine coverage of 99.6% in the habitations studied, yet only 55.1% of children demonstrated protective antibody levels — evidence, the authors concluded, that measles control in tribal areas needs attention beyond headline coverage numbers.

"Many times, explaining the importance of vaccination just once is not enough. That is why we have to visit families repeatedly to convince them about the importance of vaccination."

— Asha Maravi, Auxiliary Nurse Midwife, Balaghat

Trust, distance and mobile lives

Maravi covers nine villages spread over 40–45 km of forest; some villages are three or four kilometres from the road, so she and the ASHA workers who support her travel on foot. Rita Uike, an ANM serving several villages of Baihar block, said most Baiga families do opt to vaccinate, but trust is easily lost: when a child develops a fever or swelling after a vaccination, elders often become distressed, and some families hesitate to bring the child back for the next dose. Seasonal migration is another hurdle — families move for work in chilli fields or to cities such as Hyderabad, and children are often unavailable on scheduled vaccination dates.

"There are various challenges regarding immunisation within tribal communities. Language barriers, in particular, pose a significant problem," said Dr Saurabh Purohit, Deputy Director of the Routine Immunization programme in Madhya Pradesh. "Lack of participation in immunisation programmes can't be blamed on lack of awareness or unwillingness. There are several social and cultural factors at play."

The response since the outbreak

Since the outbreak, the administration has deployed 20 health teams to the area to conduct door-to-door health screenings for children. Health officials have also convened evening vaccination sessions for families in the at-risk areas, since most Baiga parents work as daily-wage labourers and cannot take time off during the day. Amulya Nidhi, national convener of the Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India, said working with trusted local figures and communicating in the local language are essential if programmes are to reach communities like the Baiga.
